summary: Extends Dual-Stack Lite by moving network address and port translation from a central tunnel concentrator out to the client. This makes provider-side state simpler. It builds on RFC 6333.

eli5.summary: Instead of one big post office doing all address swapping, each customer's router does its own, so the post office is lighter.

questions: what does the lwaftr binding table contain
subtitle: Dual-Stack Lite with the address translation moved from the provider's big box into each customer's router.

tldr.problem: In Dual-Stack Lite, the provider's central AFTR does the NAT for every customer and must track every active flow, which becomes costly to scale and creates a heavy logging burden where logging is a legal requirement.
tldr.mechanism: Lightweight 4over6 has the customer's router (the lwB4) do the NAPT44 using a public IPv4 address and a restricted port set it is given, while the central lwAFTR only keeps one binding entry per subscriber and encapsulates and decapsulates packets.
tldr.outcome: The provider keeps per-subscriber state instead of per-flow state and needs no central NAT44 function, at the cost of keeping provisioning and the lwAFTR binding table in sync and of each customer having a limited set of ports.

facts.label: Binding table entry
facts.value: IPv6 address, IPv4 address, port set

today: RFC 7596 is a Proposed Standard, and the metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It is a companion to RFC 7597 (MAP-E), which the text describes as offering similar capabilities with an algorithmic relationship between IPv6 and IPv4 addresses.

sections.title: Why Move the NAT to the Customer
sections.content:
Dual-Stack Lite (DS-Lite, RFC 6333) carries IPv4 over an IPv6 network using IP-in-IP tunneling and NAT. Its B4 element sits in the customer's device and builds an IPv4-in-IPv6 tunnel to an AFTR, which combines a tunnel endpoint with an IPv4-to-IPv4 NAT.

Because the AFTR does the NAT, it has to keep per-flow state for every active NAPT session. For providers with many B4 clients, the RFC says the size and cost of scaling the AFTR can quickly become prohibitive, and the per-flow state can create a large logging overhead where logging is a legal requirement.

This RFC, Lightweight 4over6 (lw4o6), relocates the NAPT function to the B4s. NAPT44 is already widely supported in customer devices, the central state shrinks from per-flow to per-subscriber, and the logging overhead drops. The tunneling mechanism itself stays the same as in DS-Lite; the changes are mostly about configuration parameters and provisioning.
sections.eli5: A big central office was tracking every single conversation for every customer. Now each customer's own router tracks its conversations, and the office just keeps a short list of customers.

sections.title: The Architecture: lwB4, lwAFTR and Provisioning
sections.content:
Like DS-Lite, lw4o6 uses an IPv4-in-IPv6 tunnel between customer devices and a central tunnel endpoint over an IPv6-enabled network. There are three components:

  • The lwB4, which does NAPT44 plus IPv4/IPv6 encapsulation and decapsulation.
  • The lwAFTR, which does only encapsulation and decapsulation and keeps per-subscriber address bindings, with no NAPT44.
  • A provisioning system that tells the lwB4 which public IPv4 address and port set to use, for example through DHCP, the Port Control Protocol or TR-69.

The lwAFTR needs the binding between each subscriber's IPv6 address and the IPv4 address and port set allocated to them. It uses this for ingress filtering upstream and encapsulation downstream. The information in the provisioning system and in the lwAFTR MUST be synchronized, although how that happens is out of scope.

A restricted port set is a non-overlapping range of external ports given to an lwB4, and a port-restricted IPv4 address is a public address with such a port set, so several B4s can share one address. Unlike RFC 7040, which assigns only a full IPv4 address, lw4o6 allows either a full or a shared address.
sections.eli5: Many houses can share one public street number as long as each house is given its own range of door numbers. The post office keeps a list of who owns which range.

sections.title: Provisioning the lwB4
sections.content:
Plain DS-Lite needs only the IPv6 address of the AFTR. An lwB4 needs four parameters: the lwAFTR's IPv6 address, the public IPv4 address for NAPT44, the restricted port set, and an IPv6 binding prefix.

The lwB4 MUST implement DHCPv6 configuration using OPTION_S46_CONT_LW from RFC 7598, so the softwire's lifetime is tied to the DHCPv6 lease. If stateful IPv4 configuration or extra IPv4 information is needed, DHCP 4o6 (RFC 7341) MUST be used. The document covers only a single tunnel.

The lwB4 does a longest-prefix match between the binding prefix and its active IPv6 prefixes to pick the tunnel source subnet, then builds the full /128 source address the same way as RFC 7597. If that source address changes, for example when the DHCPv6 lease expires, provisioning MUST be redone. If the public IPv4 address or Port Set ID changes, the lwB4 MUST flush its NAPT table.

The lwB4 MUST support dynamic port-restricted address provisioning using the port-set algorithm of RFC 7597 Section 5.1, and the number of a-bits SHOULD be 0, giving one contiguous port set. Unless a full IPv4 address is allocated, PSIDs containing the system ports (0-1023) are RECOMMENDED not to be allocated.

DHCPv6 gives the client a single PSID and cannot ask for more ports. A client using all its ports may be unable to open new outbound connections. Other mechanisms, such as a PCP-based one, can provide that function.
sections.eli5: Before the router can do its job it needs to be told four things: where the central office is, which public address it may use, which range of door numbers it owns, and which prefix to use as its return address.

sections.title: Data Plane: lwB4 and lwAFTR
sections.content:
When the lwB4 gets an IPv4 packet from a host on the customer LAN (which uses an RFC 1918 address), it runs NAPT44 on the source address and port, using the public IPv4 address and a port from its allocated set. It then wraps the packet in an IPv6 header addressed from its tunnel endpoint to the lwAFTR. In the other direction it decapsulates and applies NAPT44 to the destination using its local table. It MUST discard packets whose IPv6 source is not the configured lwAFTR address, and MUST drop decapsulated packets whose IPv4 destination address or port does not match its configuration. The lwB4 is also responsible for ALGs and NAT traversal such as UPnP IGD, NAT-PMP or PCP, if needed.

The lwAFTR does no NAPT. For an outbound tunneled packet, it decapsulates it and checks that the source IPv4 and IPv6 addresses match one binding entry and that the source port is in that entry's port set. If so it forwards the packet; if not it MUST discard it or apply a policy such as redirection. For inbound IPv4 packets it looks up the destination address and port in the binding table, encapsulates toward the matching lwB4's IPv6 address, or MUST discard the packet if there is no match. The lwAFTR MUST support hairpinning between two lwB4s, and the hairpinning policy MUST be configurable.

Both elements MUST implement the common encapsulation, fragmentation and tunneling sections of RFC 6333. The lwB4's NAPT44 MUST follow the NAT behavior requirements in RFC 4787, RFC 5508 and RFC 5382.
sections.eli5: The home router swaps the public door number and puts the letter in an IPv6 envelope. The central office checks its list to see that the sender owns that door number, then opens the envelope and passes the letter on.

sections.title: The Binding Table
sections.content:
The lwAFTR keeps an address binding table. Each entry is a 3-tuple: the IPv6 address of a single lwB4, the public IPv4 address, and the restricted port set. This replaces the 5-tuple NAPT table of the DS-Lite AFTR from RFC 6333.

An entry has two jobs: encapsulating inbound IPv4 packets toward the right lwB4, and validating outbound IPv4-in-IPv6 packets before decapsulation. The lwAFTR needs no session entries.

The table MUST be synchronized with the port-restricted address provisioning process. If the lwAFTR takes part in provisioning, the table MUST be created as part of that process. Otherwise the binding MUST be synchronized another way, such as an out-of-band static update. In all cases entry lifetimes MUST be synchronized with the lifetimes of the address allocations.

The RFC also lists other provisioning options that MAY be implemented: DHCPv4 over DHCPv6 and a PCP port-set extension. It RECOMMENDS that an operator use a single provisioning mechanism, and if more than one is needed, give each a discrete set of resources.
sections.eli5: The central office's list has one line per house: the house's IPv6 address, the shared public address, and the door-number range. It does not write down each conversation.

sections.title: ICMP Handling
sections.content:
ICMPv4 does not work in an address-sharing environment without special handling, and the port-set style of sharing needs ICMP handling that DS-Lite does not. ICMPv6 MUST be handled as in RFC 2473 by both elements.

For inbound ICMP, the lwAFTR SHOULD check the ICMP type. For echo request or reply (types 8 and 0), it MUST use the ICMP Identifier as the source port to look up the binding table and forward to the stored IPv6 address, or discard the packet. For other types, it MUST find the source port in the transport header inside the ICMP data using the method in REQ-3 of RFC 5508 and look up the destination IPv4 address and that port. All other inbound ICMPv4 MUST be discarded.

For echo requests from the private network, the lwB4 SHOULD use an available port from its port set as the ICMP identifier. The lwAFTR can send ICMPv6 Type 1, Code 5 to an lwB4 when no binding matches; the lwB4 then MAY restart provisioning, and MUST discard such a message whose source is not the configured lwAFTR address.
sections.eli5: Error notes and pings also need to find the right house. The office reads the number inside the note to see which door range it belongs to.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
When a subscriber's port space shrinks because of address sharing, their port numbers become less random. That makes it much easier for an attacker to guess a port, which could lead to throughput reduction, broken connections or data corruption.

Contiguous port sets do not reduce this threat. Non-contiguous, pseudorandomly generated port sets improve randomness, provided the attacker is outside the lw4o6 domain and does not know the generation algorithm.

The lwAFTR MUST rate-limit the ICMPv6 error messages it sends, to defend against DoS attacks by an abusive user. General address-sharing issues are covered in RFC 6269, and the security considerations of whatever provisioning protocol is used also apply. Operators can use network ingress filtering (RFC 2827) to stop forged ICMP messages that spoof the lwAFTR address.
sections.eli5: If your door-number range is small, a stranger has an easier time guessing a number that works. So the office limits how many error notes it sends, so nobody can flood a house with them.
